pairs.rationale: Exodus commands a sanctuary and its vessels made according to the pattern shown on the mountain. These earthly construction instructions supply background for Hebrews' first-covenant sanctuary and worship regulations; Exodus does not call this covenant first in the selected passage.

Exodus places the table and bread of the Presence outside the veil and describes the lampstand and its lamps. Hebrews summarizes these furnishings as lampstand, table, and presentation of loaves in the first tent, called the Holy Place.

Exodus prescribes the veil and expressly says it divides the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies, with the ark within. Hebrews identifies the area behind the second curtain as the tent called the Holy of Holies.

Exodus describes the gold-covered incense altar and places it opposite the veil. Hebrews describes the inner tent as having a golden incense altar. The object and gold correspond, while the differing placement language is preserved rather than reconciled by changing altar to censer.

Exodus prescribes an ark overlaid with pure gold outside and inside and directs that the testimonies be put into it. This corresponds to Hebrews' gold-covered ark of the covenant; Exodus does not list all three contents named by Hebrews in this range.

Exodus names a golden jar filled with manna and directs its preservation before God and before the Testimony. Hebrews lists a golden jar of manna in its ark-content statement; before and in remain distinct placement descriptions.

Numbers 17:23-25 records Aaron's sprouted staff, its shoot, blossoms and nuts, and its preservation before the testimonies. Hebrews names the sprouted rod among the ark contents; the target's before-placement and nuts wording are preserved.

Deuteronomy explicitly says the tablets were put into the ark and remained there as commanded. This directly corresponds to the tablets named among Hebrews' ark contents; the selected Deuteronomy verse does not describe the manna jar or rod.

Exodus describes the cherubim above the ark, their wings overshadowing the cover, and the cover's placement. Hebrews briefly names this arrangement before declining detailed exposition; its atonement cover and Exodus' propitiatory cover retain their respective labels.

Exodus prescribes a continually burning lamp outside the veil, with Aaron and his sons tending its burning from evening to morning. This supplies a concrete recurring outer-tent service behind Hebrews' summary of continual priestly worship, rather than a complete list of those acts.

Leviticus describes blood brought within the veil and excludes anyone else from the tent during atonement for the officiant, his house and Israel. Hebrews summarizes the high priest's sole annual blood entry; the annual rule is also explicit in the separately read Leviticus 16:34.

The later passage describes confidence for entry in Jesus' blood through the new living way inaugurated through the curtain. This contrasts with the source's undisclosed way while the first tent stands; the Holy Spirit's indication is the source's own formulation.

The later passage likewise says repeated sacrifices cannot perfect those approaching and reasons about worshipers' consciousness of sins. Hebrews 9:9 specifies perfection with respect to conscience; consciousness of sins is retained as the later wording.

Colossians likewise connects eating and drinking disputes with shadow language and Christ, while also naming festivals, new moons and Sabbaths. Hebrews names foods, drinks and washings as time-limited fleshly regulations; the settings and complete lists are not equated.

The earlier passage describes the true tent pitched by the Lord rather than a human. The source describes Christ's greater and more perfect tent, not made by hands and not of this creation; its good things that have come to be is retained without being changed to a future expression.

Both emphasize once-for-all efficacy: the source describes entry through His own blood and eternal redemption, while the later passage describes sanctification through the offering of Jesus Christ's body. Blood, body, redemption and sanctification retain their respective formulations.

Leviticus describes sprinkling calf's blood and the male young goat's blood at the propitiatory cover in the holy-place atonement rite. Hebrews speaks of goats and bulls and fleshly cleanness; this is sacrificial-blood background, not identical animal-label or cleansing-object wording.

Numbers prescribes keeping the heifer's ashes for water of sprinkling as a means of purification, corresponding to Hebrews' heifer-ash cleansing example. The separately read Numbers 19:17-19 describes ashes mixed with living water and sprinkling people, distinguishing this from the blood rite.

Both describe Christ's blood with unblemished sacrificial imagery. Peter describes ransom from ancestral futile conduct; Hebrews describes His self-offering through an eternal Spirit to God and cleansing conscience from dead works for service. These agency and benefit formulations remain distinct.

Jesus' cup saying names the new covenant in His blood poured out for you. Hebrews names the new-covenant mediator and death for redemption under the first covenant, adding eternal inheritance; the single Luke verse does not state that full inheritance argument.

The following sentence explains the death requirement by the testament taking effect at death rather than while its maker lives. These are joined stages of Hebrews' own argument; the link does not add an independent legal code.

The preceding sentence introduces the requirement that the testament maker's death be established; the source gives the death-versus-living explanation. The English testament terminology is retained rather than silently replacing it with the surrounding covenant terminology.

Exodus records covenant blood assigned to the altar and sprinkled over the people, with the covenant book read aloud. This supplies the inauguration narrative behind Hebrews' statement that even the first covenant was not inaugurated without blood.

Exodus records calves, blood at the altar and over the people, and the covenant book being read. Hebrews additionally specifies goats, water, scarlet wool, hyssop, and sprinkling the book itself; the selected Exodus passage does not report all those features.

Exodus supplies Moses' blood-of-the-covenant declaration. Hebrews prints This is and God commanded for you, while Exodus prints Behold and the Lord has made with you concerning all these words; the two formulations are not treated as verbally identical.

Leviticus names Moses, the tent and utensils in consecration with anointing oil, including sprinkling the altar and anointing the tent. Hebrews specifies blood sprinkled on the tent and ministry vessels. This compares sanctuary consecration while preserving the differing material and action-object wording.

Leviticus gives blood upon the altar for atonement in place of life. Hebrews connects lawful cleansing and forgiveness with blood, retaining its almost-everything qualifier for cleansing and its separate statement about shedding blood and forgiveness.

The earlier copy-and-shadow description identifies the earthly service patterned on heavenly things. Hebrews 9:23 develops that distinction through cleansing copies and better sacrifices for heavenly things; the earlier target does not itself describe heavenly cleansing.

Romans locates the risen Christ at God's right hand interceding for us. Hebrews describes Christ entering heaven itself to appear before God's face on our behalf; the shared representation theme retains the distinct place and action formulations.

Leviticus expressly commands atonement for Israel once in the year. Hebrews uses the high priest's yearly entry with another's blood as the contrast to Christ's not entering to offer Himself repeatedly; the statutory pattern and Christ's action are distinct.

The later passage likewise describes one sacrifice for sins for all time rather than daily repetition. The source describes appearing once at the end of the ages through His sacrifice; its temporal phrase is not replaced with the target's for-all-time wording.

Both state the prospect of judgment. Corinthians specifies Christ's judgment seat and recompense for what each has done through the body; Hebrews also orders death then judgment, an order not expressly stated in the selected Corinthians verse.

Isaiah describes the one delivered to death as bearing the sins of many and being delivered up for their sins. Hebrews applies sin-bearing language to Christ's once offering, then adds His second appearance for awaiting people; the selected Isaiah verse does not state that second appearance.

Philippians describes eagerly awaiting the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, from the heavens. This corresponds to Hebrews' awaiting-Christ salvation expectation; Hebrews additionally specifies His second appearance apart from sin, which the selected Philippians verse does not state.
